analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits for everyone and funds them by taxing income above $400,000 and slowly raising the payroll tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised Social Security benefits and asked high earners to pay more, sat in committee for the rest of the 115th Congress and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have increased Social Security checks for every beneficiary and tied annual inflation increases to a price index for elderly consumers, which typically rises faster than the index now used. It would have created a higher minimum benefit for people who worked 30 or more years at low wages, raised the income levels at which Social Security benefits become taxable, and made sure new benefits couldn't cost anyone their Medicaid or disability payments. To pay for it, income above $400,000 would count for Social Security taxes and benefits for the first time, and the payroll tax rate would rise very gradually from 6.2% to 7.4% for workers and employers over about 25 years.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries — retirees, people with disabilities, and survivors — all of whom would get a benefit increase and a cost-of-living adjustment that better reflects what seniors actually spend, especially on health care. Low-wage workers with long careers would see the biggest relative gain from the new minimum benefit tied to the poverty line. Middle-income retirees would also pay less tax on their benefits, and employers would know the payroll tax path decades in advance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries, especially low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises every beneficiary's check with an across-the-board increase (the benefit formula goes from 90% to 93% of average earnings).
Uses a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers to calculate annual cost-of-living increases, better matching the higher share of income seniors spend on health care.
Creates a new minimum benefit based on years worked — rising to 125% of the poverty line for someone with 30 or more years of work — so that long careers no longer leave people below poverty.
Raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable to $50,000 for individuals and $100,000 for joint filers, shielding middle-income retirees from that tax.
Keeps the increased benefits from counting as income for Medicaid, CHIP, and SSI eligibility, so the raise cannot disqualify anyone from those programs.
Keeps the trust fund solvent past its projected exhaustion date, protecting benefits from across-the-board cuts projected for the mid-2030s under current law.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on people earning over $400,000 a year, who would pay Social Security tax on income currently exempt above the wage cap (about $127,200 in 2017), and on employers, who would pay a matching share of the gradually rising payroll tax rate. Rank-and-file workers would see their payroll tax rate rise about 0.05 percentage points per year starting in 2019, though the employer portion is widely understood to be partly shifted onto workers over time.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises payroll taxes for virtually every worker and employer, in small annual steps from 6.2% to 7.4% after 2043 — a cost that shows up in paychecks and in what employers can offer.
Higher payroll costs fall partly on employers, which critics argue can slow hiring or wage growth, though the increase is spread over decades.

By extending payroll taxation above $400,000 and using the poverty line for the new minimum benefit, the bill shifts Social Security somewhat away from its traditional structure, where benefits track taxes paid, toward a system with more redistribution — a change some object to on principle.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: higher checks, a faster-growing inflation index, a higher minimum benefit that would lift lifetime low earners, and lower income taxes on beneficiaries, paid for by asking the highest earners to contribute for the full year and by gradually raising the payroll rate by a quarter point per decade — an increase that amounts to about 20 cents per $100 of wages for both worker and employer once fully phased in. The main cost falls on employers, who would owe the matching half of the payroll increase, and on households earning over $400,000. The bill leaves the retirement age and the basic benefit structure untouched, so it avoids the cuts-to-fix approach, but its gradual tax phase-in means a small annual drag on wage growth for decades; that trade is modest compared to the benefit improvements.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees, then to subcommittees, and no committee ever voted on it or scheduled it for a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 5, 2017 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee plus two others.
Its only further actions were referrals to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Health in April 2017.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019 with the bill still in committee.
It had 174 cosponsors, all Democrats, which was not enough to overcome the Ways and Means Committee's refusal to act.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and their employers, who were spared the new taxes on income above $400,000 and the phased-in rate increase, while seniors and disabled workers went without the higher benefits the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners spared the new taxes

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security 2100 Act and recruited 174 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 174 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, roughly three-quarters of the House Democratic caucus.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Social Security
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill after referral, leaving it in subcommittee for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House floor agenda during the 115th Congress and never brought the bill up for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 174 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and with Republicans controlling the House, Ways and Means, and the floor agenda, the bill never moved.

industries.note: For the first time since 1983, their earnings above $400,000 would be subject to Social Security payroll taxes, with no matching benefit increase beyond a small 2% benefit credit on that income. The 115th Congress never acted, leaving their contributions capped.

The employer share of Social Security payroll tax would rise gradually from 6.2% to 7.4% after 2041, though only on the first $400,000 of any employee's pay. Wage growth for workers would be slightly constrained.

They would gain from higher checks and better inflation indexing, but this is the group whose interests the bill serves rather than an industry — listed here because they are the beneficiaries of the shift in payroll taxation.
